Engaging with Indigenous resurgence extends these observations by highlighting the local turn’s lacuna around Indigenous peacebuilding within settler-colonial contexts and linking this blind spot to the local turn’s conceptual contradistinction between intervention and indigeneity.

Despite thoroughgoing critiques of the form and function of liberal peacebuilding interventions, there remains a real sense among local turn scholars that such interventions – and resulting processes of hybridization – still represent the most viable path toward the emancipation of marginalized groups (Sabaratnam 2011; Richmond and Mitchell 2012). On the one hand, peacebuilding interventions are viewed as necessary insofar as the brute fact of violent conflict signals a failure of local peacebuilding capabilities (Sabaratnam 2013; Nadarajah and Rampton 2015). Because positive hybrid peace outcomes depend on interventions following perceived failures of local peacebuilding efforts, local turn advocates frankly assert that ‘the subaltern requires intervention to modify the otherwise immutable structures of domination they face’ (Richmond 2017, 1017, emphasis added). Local resistance to liberal intervention in turn creates a potential ‘location of emancipatory knowledge and practice that [can] challenge structures of international inequality and conflict’ (Lewis 2017, 26).

As resurgence advocates explain, this discursive de-localization of violence by liberal settler-colonial states functions as ‘a way of avoiding complicity … a way of recasting the gaze. It’s like, ‘We’re not going to look right here, because this appears to be fairly peaceful’ … [So] it’s always that sort of re-directing away from localized responsibility’ (Snelgrove, Dhamoon, and Corntassel 2014, 22). This trap is particularly dangerous for Peace Studies scholars located in settler-colonial states, as the field’s normative commitment to reducing violence on a global scale can function as a ‘settler move to innocence’ that masks complicity in settler-colonial violence closer to home (Goetze 2016; Tuck and Yang 2012).

While conceding that ‘the materiality of territory may play a role’ in some accounts of the local, Mac Ginty has responded to similar concerns by suggesting ‘a post-territorial view’ of the local that should ‘regard the local as activity and interpret it according to its deeds, actions and capabilities’ as opposed to its geographical location (Mac Ginty 2015, 848; Richmond 2011b, 2015). While disengaging ‘the local’ from specific geographies might satisfy some critics of the local turn’s liberal/local binary, it also risks further obscuring Indigenous land claims associated with grounded conceptions of peace.
